title: Tame inertia implies a surjective group trace
statement: Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let a finite group $G$ act on $R$ by ring automorphisms. Write $A=R^G=\{r\in R:g(r)=r\text{ for all }g\in G\}$. For each prime ideal $\mathfrak p\subset R$, let $\kappa(\mathfrak p)=R_{\mathfrak p}/\mathfrak pR_{\mathfrak p}$ [def-weil-pbc-localization-at-prime] and define its inertia subgroup by $I_{\mathfrak p}=\{g\in G:g(\mathfrak p)=\mathfrak p\text{ and }g\text{ induces the identity on }\kappa(\mathfrak p)\}$. Assume $|I_{\mathfrak p}|$ is invertible in $\kappa(\mathfrak p)$ for every prime $\mathfrak p$. Then the $A$-linear group trace $T:R\to A$, $T(r)=\sum_{g\in G}g(r)$, is surjective; equivalently, there is $a\in R$ with $\sum_{g\in G}g(a)=1$. No Noetherian or finite-type hypothesis is imposed.

source.place: Tags 0BRH (lemma-base-change-invariants), 0BRI (lemma-one-orbit), and 0BRJ (lemma-one-orbit-geometric): localization and orbit input for the agent-supplied semilocal trace argument, written in report.md. This is a consequence, not a verbatim statement of these tags.

proof.text: For $h\in G$, left multiplication $g\mapsto hg$ permutes $G$, so $h(T(r))=T(r)$. Thus $T$ takes values in $A$. For $a\in A$, $T(ar)=aT(r)$, and $T(r+r^\prime)=T(r)+T(r^\prime)$. Consequently $J=T(R)$ is an ideal of $A$. It suffices to show that $J$ is contained in no maximal ideal of $A$.

source.place: Tag 0BRH, lemma-base-change-invariants: fixed-ring notation; elementary group-sum calculation supplied by the worker.

proof.text: For each $r\in R$, the monic polynomial $P_r(X)=\prod_{g\in G}(X-g(r))$ has coefficients in $A$: applying any $h\in G$ just permutes its factors. Since the identity factor vanishes at $r$, $P_r(r)=0$. Hence the inclusion $A\hookrightarrow R$ is integral, meaning that each element of $R$ satisfies a monic polynomial over $A$. No finite-generation assumption is used.

source.place: Tag 0BRI, lemma-one-orbit, first two sentences of the proof (orbit polynomial).

proof.text: Fix a maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$ of $A$. The inclusion $A\hookrightarrow R$ is injective and integral by Step 2. Lying over gives a prime $\mathfrak p$ of $R$ with $\mathfrak p\cap A=\mathfrak m$. The prime-over-maximal lemma then makes $\mathfrak p$ maximal. Every ideal $g(\mathfrak p)$ is maximal because $g$ is an automorphism; the set $\mathcal O=\{g(\mathfrak p):g\in G\}$ is finite.

source.place: Tag 00GQ, lemma-integral-overring-surjective, and Tag 00GS, lemma-integral-over-field, part (3).

proof.text: Put $k=R/\mathfrak p$. For $s\notin\mathfrak p$, maximality gives $\mathfrak p+(s)=R$, hence $us+v=1$ for some $u\in R$ and $v\in\mathfrak p$; thus $\bar u$ is the inverse of $\bar s$. Consequently $k$ is a field and agrees canonically with $\kappa(\mathfrak p)$: the localization formula sends $r/s$ to $\bar r\,\bar s^{-1}$, and its inverse sends $\bar r$ to the class of $r/1$. These maps are inverse because $s\notin\mathfrak p$ has nonzero, hence invertible, image in $k$. Put $D=\{g:g(\mathfrak p)=\mathfrak p\}$ and let $H$ be the image of $D$ in $\operatorname{Aut}(k)$. This is a nonempty finite set of distinct automorphisms. The kernel of $D\to H$ is exactly $I_{\mathfrak p}$ under the displayed identification. For each $\sigma\in H$, choose a lift $d\in D$; its entire fiber is the coset $dI_{\mathfrak p}$, since two lifts differ by an element of the kernel. Thus every fiber has $|I_{\mathfrak p}|$ elements.

source.place: Tag 0BRJ, lemma-one-orbit-geometric: decomposition group and residue-field notation; the maximal-residue identification and kernel-coset count are written out here.

proof.text: Apply independence of multiplicative characters with $M$ the multiplicative monoid of $k$, $L=k$, and the finite list of distinct maps $\sigma\in H$. They are monoid homomorphisms because they are field automorphisms. Their sum cannot be the zero function: otherwise the relation with every coefficient equal to $1$ contradicts independence, since $H$ contains the identity and $1\ne0$ in $k$. Choose $b\in k$ such that $u=\sum_{\sigma\in H}\sigma(b)\ne0$.

proof.text: Step 6 applies to every maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$ of $A$, so no such ideal contains $J$. If $J\ne A$, the proper-ideal maximal-ideal lemma would give a maximal ideal containing $J$, a contradiction. Therefore $J=A$. In particular $1=T(a)$ for some $a\in R$, and then every $c\in A$ equals $T(ca)$ by $A$-linearity. Conversely surjectivity gives a preimage of $1$. This also handles the zero ring: there $J=A$ and $T(0)=0=1$, with no maximal ideals to consider.
